explain.say: Under the platform of a digital scale is a load cell, a small metal bar fixed at one end. When you put food on, it bends by a tiny amount, far too little to see.

explain.say: The more weight, the more bending, so the chip turns the reading into grams on the display. Pressing tare simply sets the current weight to zero, so you can weigh food in a bowl.

faq.a: A load cell is a metal block or bar designed to bend very slightly under weight, with strain gauges attached that measure the bend.
asks: How does a digital scale work?

faq.a: A strain gauge is a thin zigzag of metal foil on a backing. When it is stretched or squashed, its electrical resistance changes slightly, which can be measured.
asks: How does a strain gauge measure force?

faq.q: What does the tare button do?
faq.a: Tare tells the scale to treat what is already on it, like an empty bowl, as zero. Then the display shows only the weight of what you add.
asks: Why do you press zero before weighing?

faq.q: Why does a scale need to be on a flat surface?
faq.a: The load cell is designed to be pushed straight down. On a slope or a soft surface, some of the weight pushes sideways or the feet rock, giving a wrong reading.
asks: Why does my scale give different readings?

faq.q: Does a scale measure mass or weight?
faq.a: It measures the force of the food pushing down, its weight, then shows it as grams of mass. On the Moon the same scale would read about one sixth as much.
asks: Would a kitchen scale work on the Moon?

facts: Strain gauges change their electrical resistance when stretched, which lets them measure tiny bends.
The bonded metal foil strain gauge was developed in the late 1930s by Edward Simmons and Arthur Ruge.
